subject: A toy example where nondiagonal matrix outperforms the default stan

messages.author: ace9745b50e86915
messages.subject: A toy example where nondiagonal matrix outperforms the default stan
parts:
Hi everyone!

I implemented a sampling method which uses a given (nondiagonal) covariance matrix to perform NUTS. A toy example shows that this method can be faster than the default one we are using by reducing the number of leapfrogs needed in each iteration. I attach the result in pdf.

The example is quite trivial and extreme... But I feel it is illustrative and this is what I can do right now with 2 finals next week... Hope that you can give some comments about the result. Thanks a lot.

Best,
Yuanjun

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] A toy example where nondiagonal matrix outperforms the default stan
parts:
Yuanjun,

Great work.

Clock ticks are CPU cycles -- you can convert to time by using the "CLOCKS_PER_SEC" macro. For example,

clock_t start = clock();
// Do something
clock_t end = clock();

double deltaT = (double)(end - start) / CLOCKS_PER_SEC

I'd actually be interested to see a high dimensional example. From my experience with RMHMC the pathologies in high-dimensional likelihoods actually scale worse than N^{2}, so the dense mass matrix can still be beneficial.

-Mike

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] A toy example where nondiagonal matrix outperforms the default stan
parts:
Those autocorrelation plots in figure 2 look awesome.
This is fantastic progress -- can't wait to see what
you come up with when you're not working on finals!

If I understand what you have now in table 1, it's just
overall time for 10^5 samples and expected leapfrog
steps per sample.

I'm thinking the results are even better than your report.

What we really care about is time to useful number of
effective samples (say 100 per parameter). That means
running multiple chains (let's say 4) and making sure
all parameters pass the R-hat diagnostic test (R-hat < 1.1).

I suggest measuring the following for convergence time

1. # of iterations to converge (4 chains, all params Rhat < 1.1)
2. avg # leapfrog steps / iteration
3. cost / leapfrog step
4. => time to converge

and the following for mixing after convergence

1. # of iterations / effective sample
2. avg time / iteration
3. => time / effective sample at convergence

The more I think about things like the way our tests behave,
the more I think we need to run these multiple times with
different inits and look at variance. I wouldn't be at all
surprised if the full mass matrix turns out to be more robust
than a diagonal mass in some cases and less so in others.

The leapfrog calcs, and in particular the gradients,
do indeed dwarf the rest of the calcs being done in NUTS.

Next, I'd try to test the effect of dimensionality that
you discuss at the end of the pdf. This might also get
at the robustness.

There are really three ways to scale that we care about:

1. more data (does not increase dimensionality, does increase leapfrog time)

2. more parameters

3. more complex models (e.g., hierarchical or time series)

- Bob

Dear Bob,

Thank you very much for your reply. I am really excited when getting the autocorrelation plot. I am pretty sure that for highly correlated posterior which is close to multi-normal distribution, the dense covariance matrix will greatly improve the sampling result by "eliminating" the directions with small variance.

It's just because running multiple chains and doing analysis with command-line stan is not quite convenient that I don't want to spend that much effort on this toy example (there is no command in command-line stan which allow a multiple chain sampling right?). I'll definitely perform multiple chain analysis for a higher dimensional example which is less trivial.

Best,
Yuanjun

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] A toy example where nondiagonal matrix outperforms the default stan
parts:
On Sunday, December 16, 2012 4:04:19 PM UTC-5, Yuanjun Gao wrote:
Yes, your understanding of table 1 is correct, and I definitely agree that using multiple chains will lead to a much more comprehensive analysis. It's just because running multiple chains and doing analysis with command-line stan is not quite convenient that I don't want to spend that much effort on this toy example (there is no command in command-line stan which allow a multiple chain sampling right?). I'll definitely perform multiple chain analysis for a higher dimensional example which is less trivial.

You can do

for i in {1..4}
do
  ./model --refresh=0 --seed=12345 --chain_id=$i --samples=samples$i.csv &
done

which will background each process and essentially do four chains in parallel (assuming you have at least four cores to work with). RStan v1.0.4 has functions to read the four samples*.csv files into a stanfit object, which can calculate Rhats, n_effs, etc.

Ben
